1) Drug-associated eruptive melanocytic nevi (BRAF-inhibitor–related melanocytic proliferation)  
   - Most likely given rapid onset of multiple new dark moles within ~8 weeks of starting encorafenib (BRAF inhibitor).

2) New primary melanomas (multiple or synchronous lesions)  
   - Important to consider because melanomas can present as new pigmented lesions and BRAF inhibitors have been associated with emergence/progression of melanocytic lesions.

3) Seborrheic keratoses (eruptive SKs)  
   - Common pigmented papules on face/scalp that can appear rapidly and mimic “moles.”

4) Lentigo maligna or pigmented actinic keratoses (sun-related pigmented lesions)  
   - Especially plausible on sun-exposed face/scalp in older adults; can appear as new/dark macules.

5) Cutaneous metastases or pigmented non-melanocytic tumors (rare)  
   - Uncommon but considered because of underlying metastatic cancer; would be lower on the list.

Immediate recommended actions (clinical next steps)
- Urgent full skin examination by a dermatologist with dermoscopic imaging of representative lesions (especially any asymmetric, irregular, changing, bleeding, or rapidly growing lesions).  
- Prompt excisional or targeted punch/shave biopsy and histopathology (including melanoma immunostains S100, SOX10, Melan-A) of the most atypical lesion(s) on the scalp/face.  
- Inform your oncology team (medical oncologist) about new cutaneous lesions — consider review of current systemic therapy and need for dermatology–oncology coordination.  
- If biopsy shows atypia/melanoma, manage per melanoma staging guidelines; if benign eruptive nevi related to therapy, continue dermatologic surveillance at regular intervals (and inspect for other BRAF-inhibitor–associated lesions such as keratoacanthomas/SCCs).
